tldr: Oregon respondents across business, workforce, housing, and environmental sectors identify key competitive challenges: high taxes and the elimination of state-level QSBS treatment deter founders and early-stage tech; fragmented local permitting and fees obstruct housing production; workforce development programs lack accountability; and the Climate Protection Program imposes significant costs on energy-intensive businesses. Recommendations cluster around tax reform, building-code modernization, statewide coordination on housing, decentralized workforce development, and infrastructure investment. A minority of respondents prioritize ecological restoration and degrowth frameworks over industrial expansion.

bullets.text: Climate Protection Program (CPP) estimated to cost Oregon natural gas consumers $4.9 Billion over the 11-year period (2025–2035), cited by manufacturers as major competitive disadvantage vs. other states

Elimination of state-level QSBS treatment (SB 1507) identified by multiple founders as key factor discouraging startup formation and company retention in Oregon vs. peer states (Washington, Texas, Colorado, Massachusetts)

Housing production constrained by fragmented local permitting, system development charges (SDCs), and unpredictable fee structures; respondents call for statewide guardrails, fee caps, standardized impact analysis, and advance notice of changes

Building-code reforms (adopt ISO elevator standards, legalize interlocking stairs and single-stair buildings up to 6–8 floors) identified as levers to reduce construction costs and increase housing production at scale

Workforce development fragmented across state agencies; recommendation to divest in state-level programs, empower local workforce development boards, and adopt Texas Workforce Commission model for accountability and regional intermediaries

Small business barriers: limited access to contracts (especially public procurement), working capital lines of credit, and technical support; respondents praise Small Business TAP program and call for expansion and federal-state coordination

Tax structure concerns: Portland/Multnomah County marginal income tax rates among highest in nation; respondents call for comprehensive tax reform, possible sales tax, limits on city/county income-tax variation, and extended QSBS incentives

Biotech and innovation sector respondents request improved tax incentives, startup-retention tracking, and decentralized venture models; cite Pennsylvania's Ben Franklin Technology Partners and Maryland TEDCO as regional, hands-on alternatives

Climate and environmental-justice respondents advocate for degrowth, ecological restoration, and redirection of economic-development funds to land trusts, care work, and community health—contrasting sharply with growth-focused business-climate submissions
